analysis.one_liner: Replaces income, payroll, and estate taxes with a 23% national sales tax and abolishes the IRS.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced in January 2017 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the federal income tax, payroll taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare, and the estate and gift tax, replacing them all with a single national sales tax of 23% on nearly everything people buy. Every legal-resident household would get a monthly rebate covering the sales tax on poverty-level spending, and the states would collect the tax for the Treasury for a small fee. The IRS would lose all funding after 2021, and the sales tax would end automatically if the constitutional amendment allowing an income tax were not repealed within seven years.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households and wealthy estates gain the most: the estate and gift tax disappears, and purchases made for investment purposes — stocks, bonds, and other assets held to appreciate — are exempt from the sales tax, so wealth accumulation goes untaxed while an heir's inheritance passes free of federal tax. Workers at all income levels gain from paycheck simplicity and the monthly rebate, which shields spending up to the poverty line. Businesses gain because everything they buy for business purposes is exempt, and large sellers keep an administration credit worth up to 20% of the tax they remit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, wealthy estates, and big savers

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the income tax, the Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate and gift taxes, and abolishes funding for the IRS after fiscal year 2021, ending individual tax filing.

It replaces those taxes with a 23% national sales tax on the use or consumption of goods and services, with the rate set against gross payments so it is tax-inclusive — $23 of every $100 register total, roughly a 30% markup on the sticker price.

Every qualified family of lawful residents receives a monthly rebate (the Family Consumption Allowance) equal to the tax rate times the HHS poverty guideline for their family size, effectively refunding the sales tax on poverty-level consumption.
States that already run sales taxes administer and collect the federal tax and keep an administration fee of 0.25% of what they remit.
Purchases for business, export, or investment purposes are exempt, as is used property, so the tax falls on final consumption only.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers bear the new tax every time they buy something new: a 23% tax-inclusive rate means roughly 30 cents added to every dollar at the register. Because spending makes up a larger share of income for working and middle-class families than for the wealthy, the tax bites hardest on people who spend most of what they earn — and the rebate only covers poverty-level consumption, so a family earning well above the poverty line pays the full rate on most of its purchases. Retirees and others who already paid income tax on their savings get taxed a second time when they spend those savings, and Social Security and Medicare funding shifts from dedicated payroll taxes to annual general-revenue appropriations, making benefits subject to the yearly budget process.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone who buys new goods and services

drawbacks.text: A 23% tax-inclusive sales tax is roughly a 30% markup at the register on essentially everything new a family buys, and because consumption takes a larger share of income at the bottom and middle, the burden falls more heavily on working households; the monthly rebate shields only poverty-level spending, so a nurse or machinist earning twice the poverty line pays the full rate on most purchases.

Purchases for investment purposes are exempt and the estate and gift tax is repealed, so wealth that is accumulated, held, and passed to heirs escapes federal tax entirely while wages spent at stores are taxed at the full rate.

Repealing payroll taxes ends dedicated funding for Social Security and Medicare; the bill instead allocates sales tax revenue to the trust funds each year, leaving retirement and hospital insurance subject to annual congressional budget decisions.

The rebate requires annual registration with the administering authority, Social Security numbers for every listed family member, and certification that all members are lawful residents — and a family that fails to register on time stops receiving the rebate until it cures the lapse.

The sales tax sunsets automatically if the Sixteenth Amendment is not repealed within seven years, which no Congress has ever done — meaning the country could face pressure to amend the Constitution on a two-year deadline.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Ending tax filing is a real, widely felt benefit, and the rebate is a genuine design feature that protects the poorest households. But the core trade is structural: the bill removes taxes on income, wealth accumulation, and inheritance — the things that concentrate at the top — and taxes instead the act of spending, which dominates lower- and middle-income budgets. The estate tax repeal alone is one of the largest single transfers to the wealthiest families available to Congress. Whether the rebate makes the package progressive at the bottom is disputed, but the mix of untaxed investment buying, untaxed inheritance, and a 30% markup on retail purchases means the heaviest burden lands on consumers and the largest gain lands on the wealthy. As written, this is a badly unbalanced trade for most households.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there, with no hearing, markup, or vote, until the Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Senator Jerry Moran introduced the Fair Tax Act of 2017 in the Senate on January 3, 2017, joined by Senator David Perdue.
Four Republican senators cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on January 3, 2017 — the only action the bill ever received.
The Finance Committee took no action on the bill for the rest of the 115th Congress, and the full Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
The bill expired with the Congress; an identical proposal has been introduced repeatedly in prior and later Congresses without becoming law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the existing tax code stayed in place: working and middle-income households kept a system where tax rises with income and where Social Security and Medicare have dedicated payroll funding, and the wealthiest households kept paying the income and estate taxes this bill would have repealed. Tax preparation firms and the IRS also retained their roles. Nobody's situation changed; the main effect of the bill's death is that a large tax shift off wealth and onto consumption never occurred.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Working households, by keeping the current tax code

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so there are no roll calls to score; all five sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on.

industries.note: The bill repeals the estate and gift tax and exempts investment purchases from the sales tax, so wealth that is saved, accumulated, or inherited is never taxed, while every dollar of wages spent at a store carries roughly a 30% markup. This is the largest single gain in the bill, and it is financed by shifting the tax onto consumption.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software companies
industries.note: Repealing the income tax and defunding the IRS eliminates the annual filing market that these firms sell into. Whether the sales tax serves consumers better than the income tax is exactly the debate the bill never got to have.
States with existing sales taxes become the primary collectors of the federal tax and keep an administration fee of 0.25% of collections, adding revenue and administrative responsibility.

Retail sellers must register, collect a 23% federal tax on top of state taxes, maintain segregated tax accounts, post security bonds if they are large sellers, and face penalties for failures — but they receive an administration credit worth the greater of $200 or 0.25% of tax remitted, capped at 20% of taxes due, and tax collection fees are the bill's stated intent.

Purchases of stocks, bonds, and other financial instruments are exempt, sparing the core of the investment business, but fees for financial intermediation services are themselves newly subject to the sales tax under the bill's special rules.
